claim: LINE-1 (L1) retrotransposons represent approximately one sixth of the human genome.
source: LINE-1 (L1) retrotransposons represent approximately one sixth of the human genome, but only the human-specific L1HS-Ta subfamily acts as an endogenous mutagen in modern humans, reshaping both somatic and germline genomes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of genomics, representing established scientific knowledge about the composition of the human genome.

claim: Only the human-specific L1HS-Ta subfamily acts as an endogenous mutagen in modern humans.
source: LINE-1 (L1) retrotransposons represent approximately one sixth of the human genome, but only the human-specific L1HS-Ta subfamily acts as an endogenous mutagen in modern humans, reshaping both somatic and germline genomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about L1 retrotransposon activity in humans.

claim: Only a very restricted subset of L1HS-Ta loci significantly contributes to the bulk of L1 expression.
source: Strikingly, only a very restricted subset of L1HS-Ta loci - some being polymorphic among individuals - significantly contributes to the bulk of L1 expression, and these loci are differentially regulated among distinct cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ATLAS-seq data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: L1HS-Ta loci are differentially regulated among distinct cell lines.
source: Strikingly, only a very restricted subset of L1HS-Ta loci - some being polymorphic among individuals - significantly contributes to the bulk of L1 expression, and these loci are differentially regulated among distinct cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 4a.

claim: L1 transcriptional activation in somatic cells is governed by individual-, locus-, and cell-type-specific determinants.
source: Thus, our data support a local model of L1 transcriptional activation in somatic cells, governed by individual-, locus-, and cell-type-specific determinants.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the combined ATLAS-seq and RNA-seq data showing differential expression patterns across cell types and loci.

claim: Most L1 copies have accumulated mutations or are truncated and are unable to initiate new cycles of retrotransposition.
source: Since most copies have accumulated mutations or are truncated, they are unable to initiate new cycles of retrotransposition and could be considered as molecular fossils (although in some cases they might nevertheless still be transcriptionally active [Macia et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Macia et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The L1HS-Ta subfamily continues to retrotranspose and accumulate in modern human genomes.
source: In contrast, the youngest and human-specific L1 subfamily, 'transcribed L1, subset a' or L1HS-Ta, continues to retrotranspose and to accumulate in modern human genomes (Boissinot et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boissinot et al., 2000.

claim: Each individual has hundreds of additional L1HS-Ta copies not present in the reference genome.
source: Hence, each individual has hundreds of additional copies not present in the reference genome, referred to as 'non-reference' L1HS-Ta, which contribute to our genetic diversity (Xing et al., 2009; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009; Ewing and Kazazian, 2010; Beck et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010; Iskow et al., 2010; Kidd et al., 2010; Lupski, 2010; Ewing and Kazazian, 2011; Ray and Batzer, 2011; Stewart et al., 2011; Mir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting L1 insertional polymorphism.

claim: L1HS-Ta can mobilize in the germline, early embryo, and embryonic stem cells, resulting in inheritable genetic variations.
source: Recent advances in deep-sequencing technologies have also led to the discovery that L1HS-Ta are not only able to mobilize in the germline, in the early embryo and in embryonic stem cells - resulting in inheritable genetic variations (van den Hurk et al., 2007; Wissing et al., 2012; Hancks and Kazazian, 2012; Macia et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: L1HS-Ta can retrotranspose in some somatic tissues such as brain.
source: but can also retrotranspose in some somatic tissues such as brain (Faulkner et al., 2009; Coufal et al., 2009; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012; Erwin et al., 2014; Richardson et al., 2014; Upton et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting L1 activity in brain tissue.

claim: L1HS-Ta can retrotranspose in many epithelial cancers.
source: and in many epithelial cancers (Miki et al., 1992; Iskow et al., 2010; Solyom et al., 2012; Shukla et al., 2013; Rodić and Burns, 2013; Pitkänen et al., 2014; Helman et al., 2014; Tubio et al., 2014; Goodier, 2014; Ewing et al., 2015; Rodić et al., 2015; Doucet-O'Hare et al., 2015; Paterson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting L1 activity in cancers.

claim: L1 transcriptional activation is primarily driven by an internal promoter located within the L1 5' UTR.
source: The first step required to initiate retrotransposition of a particular L1 instance is its transcriptional activation: this is primarily driven by an internal promoter located within the L1 5' UTR (Swergold, 1990; Minakami et al., 1992; Tchénio et al., 2000; Athanikar et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: L1 transcription can be repressed by CpG methylation.
source: but can be repressed by CpG methylation (Yoder et al., 1997; Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Muotri et al., 2010; Wissing et al., 2012; Castro-Diaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Production of L1 RNA transcripts is essential for translation of L1-encoded proteins ORF1p and ORF2p.
source: Production of L1 RNA transcripts is essential both for the translation of L1-encoded proteins, ORF1p and ORF2p, which are required for retrotransposition (Moran et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moran et al., 1996.

claim: L1 RNA transcripts act as a template for reverse transcription.
source: and to act as a template for reverse transcription itself (Wei et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2001.

claim: Only a fraction of L1 elements are retrotransposition-competent when tested in cellular assays.
source: As a result, only a fraction of L1 elements are retrotransposition-competent, even when cloned in a plasmid and tested in cellular assays, with their expression driven by a strong constitutive promoter (Brouha et al., 2003; Beck et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brouha et al., 2003 and Beck et al., 2010.

claim: Retrotransposition-competent 'hot' L1 elements are highly enriched among the youngest L1HS-Ta insertions.
source: These so-called 'hot' L1 elements are highly enriched among the youngest L1HS-Ta insertions, which are polymorphic among individuals (Beck et al., 2010; Lupski, 2010; Beck et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beck et al., 2010, Lupski, 2010, and Beck et al., 2011.

claim: The study mapped the location of L1HS-Ta elements in 12 commonly-used somatic cell lines.
source: Here we comprehensively mapped fixed and polymorphic L1HS-Ta copies in 12 commonly-used somatic cell lines, and identified transcriptional and epigenetic signatures allowing the unambiguous identification of active L1HS-Ta copies in their genomic context.
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ATLAS-seq identified 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions in the 12 cell lines analyzed.
source: In total, ATLAS-seq identified 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions in the 12 cell lines analyzed, corresponding to 1633 distinct loci and including 358 full length elements (22%) (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the ATLAS-seq experimental data.

claim: Each cell line contains on average 652 (±68) L1HS-Ta copies.
source: On average (± s.d.), each cell line contains 652 (±68) L1HS-Ta copies, including 178 (±12) full-length elements.
evidence: This is directly supported by the ATLAS-seq experimental data.

claim: ATLAS-seq recovers 98% of the L1HS-Ta elements previously described as fixed in the human population.
source: ATLAS-seq recovers 98% of the L1HS-Ta elements previously described as fixed in the human population (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), showing that this mapping approach is close to being comprehensive.
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data and comparison with known fixed insertions, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: ATLAS-seq validation by PCR showed a true positive rate of 94%.
source: We validated 66/70 of the tested L1HS-Ta, giving a true positive rate of 94% (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by PCR validation experiments.

claim: Each pair of distinct diploid normal fibroblast lines differs at an average of 298 positions with regards to the presence or absence of a specific L1HS-Ta copy.
source: Finally, each pair of distinct diploid normal fibroblast lines (IMR-90, BJ and MRC-5 in our panel) differs at an average of 298 positions with regards to the presence or absence of a specific L1HS-Ta copy, in remarkable agreement with previous estimates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) (Ewing and Kazazian, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data comparing fibroblast lines and is consistent with previous estimates from Ewing and Kazazian, 2010.

claim: ORF1p was detected in whole cell extracts of half of the transformed cell lines.
source: We detected ORF1p expression in whole cell extracts of half of the transformed cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with the proportion of human tumors expressing ORF1p (Rodić et al., 2014) and with previous work (Belancio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: No ORF1p was detected in primary fibroblasts.
source: As expected, no ORF1p was detected in primary fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data in Figure 1.

claim: MCF7 and 2102Ep cells exhibit the highest levels of L1HS-Ta RNA-seq tags.
source: Consistent with L1 RNP quantification, MCF7 and 2102Ep cells exhibit the highest levels of L1HS-Ta RNA-seq tags.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: HCT 116 and primary fibroblasts (BJ, IMR-90) have extremely reduced L1HS-Ta levels.
source: Most other transformed cells have intermediate levels, while HCT 116 and primary fibroblasts (BJ, IMR-90) have extremely reduced L1HS-Ta levels (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: H1 cells express relatively high levels of L1HS-Ta.
source: In agreement with previous studies on other hESC, H1 cells express relatively high levels of L1HS-Ta (Garcia-Perez et al., 2007; Macia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to Garcia-Perez et al., 2007 and Macia et al., 2011.

claim: Only 5 L1HS-Ta copies in MCF7 cells show relatively high expression.
source: Strikingly, only 5 L1HS-Ta copies show relatively high expression, and approximately 15 more copies exhibit low but detectable levels of expression.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Only 4 L1HS-Ta loci in MCF7 cells show evidence of L1 antisense promoter activity.
source: In addition, only 4 L1HS-Ta loci show evidence of L1 antisense promoter activity, including instances that are distinct from the few copies expressing high levels of L1 sense transcripts, suggesting uncoupling and differential regulation between these two L1 promoter activities.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Transcribed L1HS-Ta loci have upstream active chromatin marks (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) and Pol-II and downstream RNA-seq signal.
source: Consistent with the examples described at the TTC28 and NEDD4 loci (Figure 3b), transcribed L1HS-Ta loci at the genome-wide level have a dual fingerprint with upstream active chromatin marks (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) and Pol-II and downstream RNA-seq signal (Figure 3f)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3b and 3f.

claim: The expression pattern of individual L1HS-Ta loci in standard growth conditions is highly reproducible.
source: The expression pattern of individual L1HS-Ta loci in standard growth conditions is highly reproducible, as revealed by the clustering of independent RNA-seq experiments obtained from the same cell line grown in two independent laboratory environments (Figure 4a, MCF7_Cristofari and MCF7_ENCODE samples, Pearson correlation r=0.830 p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis of RNA-seq data from independent experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: For most L1HS-Ta-expressing cells, only 5 to 15 individual copies contribute to the bulk of L1HS-Ta RNA.
source: Interestingly, for most L1HS-Ta-expressing cells, only 5 to 15 individual copies contribute to the bulk of L1HS-Ta RNA, defined as the number of L1 copy contributing to half of the total FPKM count (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The identity of the individual L1HS-Ta loci which are expressed varies considerably between cell types.
source: The identity of the individual L1HS-Ta loci which are expressed, as well as their levels of expression, varies considerably between cell types (Figure 4a and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Many L1HS-Ta elements present at the same genomic location in distinct cell types are differentially expressed.
source: Strikingly, many L1HS-Ta elements which are present at the same genomic location in distinct cell types are differentially expressed, indicating that L1HS-Ta re-activation in transformed cells may result from cell-type- and copy-specific regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differential expression patterns across cell types.

claim: The total levels of RNA-seq tags 1 kb downstream of L1HS-Ta are highly correlated with the number of internal L1 reads containing the ACA diagnostic nucleotides.
source: The total levels of RNA-seq tags 1 kb downstream of L1HS-Ta for a given cell line are highly correlated with the number of internal L1 reads containing the ACA diagnostic nucleotides (Spearman r=0.8169, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Approximately 1/3 of all full-length L1HS-Ta copies were inserted in genes.
source: Approximately 1/3 of all full-length L1HS-Ta copies were inserted in genes (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Genic L1 copies are more often found in the antisense orientation.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Szak et al., 2002), genic L1 copies are more often found in the antisense orientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a and is consistent with Szak et al., 2002.

claim: Genes containing expressed L1 are often more expressed than those containing non-expressed L1.
source: Independently of their orientation relative to genes, we found that genes containing expressed L1 are often more expressed than those containing non-expressed L1 (Figure 4d)
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The majority of L1 copies were inserted in normal regions (not copy number variants).
source: The majority of L1 copies were inserted in normal regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b), whether they were expressed or not, and expressed L1 copies were not significantly enriched in amplified regions.
evidence: This is supported by the copy number variation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b.

claim: At least 11 out of the 20 most highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies across all cell lines are retrotransposition-competent.
source: Thus, in total, at least 11 out of the 20 most highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies across all cell lines are retrotransposition-competent (Figure 5a and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by cellular retrotransposition assays, 3' transduction analysis, and published data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: L1HS-Ta transcription is predominantly inactive in somatic human cells, including transformed cell lines.
source: Altogether our observations support a model (Figure 6) where: (i) L1HS-Ta transcription is predominantly inactive in somatic human cells, including transformed cell lines
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive RNA-seq and ATLAS-seq data across multiple cell lines.

claim: A small number of L1HS-Ta copies can escape silencing, allowing their expression and transcript accumulation.
source: however (ii) a small number of L1HS-Ta copies can escape silencing, allowing their expression and transcript accumulation
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data showing limited number of expressed copies.

claim: The locus in which a particular L1HS copy integrates has a major influence on its ability to be subsequently reactivated.
source: (iii) the locus in which a particular L1HS copy integrates has a major influence on its ability to be subsequently reactivated
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that identical L1 copies at different loci show different expression patterns.

claim: L1 instances at distinct genomic loci are subject to cell-type dependent activation.
source: (iv) L1 instances at distinct genomic loci are subject to cell-type dependent activation (potentially dependent on environmental or physiological signals).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression patterns observed across cell types.

claim: The general cellular regulation of most L1 instances is unimpaired in cancer cell-lines studied, even in cells exhibiting high L1 activity.
source: Strikingly, our results indicate that – in the cancer cell-lines studied – the general cellular regulation of most L1 instances is unimpaired, even in cells exhibiting high L1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only a small subset of L1 copies are expressed even in high L1-expressing cancer cells.

claim: Shut-off of global L1-regulatory pathways is not a prerequisite for L1 activation in cancer.
source: Thus, it appears that shut-off of global L1-regulatory pathways is not a prerequisite for L1 activation in cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most L1 copies remain silenced even in cancer cells with high L1 activity.

claim: Only a very limited set of L1 copies, at specific genomic loci, become activated in cancer cells.
source: Instead, we find that only a very limited set of L1 copies, at specific genomic loci, become activated in cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data showing limited number of expressed L1 copies in cancer cell lines.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of human tumors has revealed recurrent retrotransposition events stemming from a handful of source elements.
source: Recently, whole genome sequencing of human tumors has revealed recurrent retrotransposition events stemming from a handful of source elements (Tubio et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tubio et al., 2014.

claim: L1 transcriptional activation is a key regulatory process which limits the mutagenic potential of L1 elements independently of their respective intrinsic biochemical activity.
source: Here, we have identified highly heterogeneous expression of individual L1HS-Ta copies, implicating L1 transcriptional activation as a key regulatory process which limits the mutagenic potential of L1 elements independently of their respective intrinsic biochemical activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many retrotransposition-competent L1 copies are not expressed.

claim: L1-mediated mutagenesis results from the reactivation of a small subset of permissive loci, only a fraction of which contains retrotransposition-competent elements.
source: We conclude that L1-mediated mutagenesis results from the reactivation of a small subset of permissive loci, only a fraction of which contains retrotransposition-competent elements, combined with a favorable cellular environment (i.e. diminished restriction factor and/or increased cofactor activities [Pizarro and Cristofari, 2016]).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on L1 expression and retrotransposition competence.

claim: Several of the regulated L1 loci are polymorphic with regards to the presence or absence of an L1 element among the human population.
source: Several of these regulated loci are polymorphic with regards to the presence or absence of an L1 element among the human population, highlighting the role of genetic determinants in the global L1 mutagenic potential in a given individual.
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data showing polymorphic L1 insertions among cell lines.

claim: The weak L1 polyadenylation signal in the 3' UTR allows a fraction of L1 transcripts to extend into the downstream genomic sequence.
source: To gain insight into the pattern of L1 expression in human somatic cells at single copy resolution, we noted that the weak L1 polyadenylation signal in the 3' UTR allows a fraction of L1 transcripts to extend into the downstream genomic sequence (Holmes et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holmes et al., 1994.

claim: The L1 antisense promoter activity generates antisense transcripts extending into the upstream genomic region flanking the L1 element.
source: Similarly, the L1 antisense promoter activity generates antisense transcripts extending into the upstream genomic region flanking the L1 element (Speek, 2001; Cruickshanks and Tufarelli, 2009; Rangwala et al., 2009; Macia et al., 2011; Denli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two different ORF1 shRNAs greatly reduced the downstream RNA-seq signal when compared to a scrambled shRNA or to unmanipulated cells.
source: Second, we performed shRNA-mediated knockdown of all L1HS-Ta transcripts, targeting the ORF1 sequence (Figure 3c). Two different ORF1 shRNAs greatly reduced the downstream RNA-seq signal when compared to a scrambled shRNA or to unmanipulated cells (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: Downstream RNA-seq tags originate from the same transcriptional unit as the considered L1.
source: Together, these data indicate that downstream RNA-seq tags originate from the same transcriptional unit as the considered L1.
evidence: This is inferred from the H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data and shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The concomitant presence of an upstream H3K4me3 mark at many transcriptionally active L1 copies renders the possibility of 3' transduction very unlikely in most cases.
source: However, the concomitant presence of an upstream H3K4me3 mark at many transcriptionally active L1 copies renders this situation very unlikely in most cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing H3K4me3 marks at expressed L1 loci.

claim: Sense and antisense L1 promoter activities are not necessarily coupled in a chromosomal environment.
source: Interestingly, in both cases, we do not detect upstream antisense RNA-seq tags at the vicinity of these full-length L1HS-Ta copies, suggesting that sense and antisense L1 promoter activities - or the stability of their respective transcripts - are not necessarily coupled in a chromosomal environment, in agreement with previous results obtained from plasmid borne reporter assays (Macia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data and is consistent with Macia et al., 2011.

claim: The human reference genome hg19 contains 485 L1HS-Ta insertions with a detectable 3' end.
source: The human reference genome hg19 contains 485 L1HS-Ta insertions with a detectable 3' end.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the reference genome.

claim: On average, each cell line contains 393 (±10) reference insertions, 179 (±18) non-reference L1HS-Ta previously identified as L1 insertion polymorphisms, and 80 (±60) novel insertions.
source: Among them 393 (±10) are reference insertions, 179 (±18) are non-reference L1HS-Ta previously identified as L1 insertion polymorphisms and catalogued in euL1db (Mir et al., 2015), and 80 (±60) are novel insertions (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: One fifth of the L1 loci are present in all tested cell lines.
source: One fifth of the L1 loci are present in all tested cell lines and approximately 40% of them are present in only one of the cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data showing L1 polymorphism among cell lines.

claim: Approximately 40% of L1 loci are present in only one of the cell lines.
source: One fifth of the L1 loci are present in all tested cell lines and approximately 40% of them are present in only one of the cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the ATLAS-seq data showing L1 polymorphism among cell lines.

claim: Full-length L1 elements contain internal sense and antisense promoters located in their 5'-untranslated region (UTR).
source: Full-length L1 elements contain internal sense and antisense promoters located in their 5'-untranslated region (UTR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L1 structure.

claim: ORF1p associates with the L1 mRNA and L1 ORF2p to form a ribonucleoprotein particle (RNP) which mediates the retrotransposition reaction.
source: ORF1p associates with the L1 mRNA, and L1 ORF2p, to form a ribonucleoprotein particle (RNP), which mediates the retrotransposition reaction (Kulpa and Moran, 2006; Doucet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kulpa and Moran, 2006 and Doucet et al., 2010.

claim: L1-derived RNA-transcripts and proteins are detected in embryonic stem cells, embryonal carcinoma cells, and other transformed cells or tumors, as well as in neuronal progenitor cells, but not in most primary cells.
source: Human L1-derived RNA-transcripts and proteins, required for L1 retrotransposition, are detected in embryonic stem cells, in embryonal carcinoma cells, and other transformed cells or tumors, as well as in neuronal progenitor cells, but not in most primary cells, such as fibroblasts (Faulkner et al., 2009; Coufal et al., 2009; Belancio et al., 2010; Wissing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study selected twelve widely used cell lines belonging to different categories for analysis.
source: To study the polymorphism and expression of the L1HS-Ta subfamily at the level of individual genomic instances, we selected twelve widely used cell lines belonging to each of these different categories (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Ten of the cell lines have been characterized in depth as part of the ENCODE project.
source: These included 10 cell lines which have been characterized in depth as part of the ENCODE project (Bernstein et al., 2012), together with two others – the commonly used embryonic lung fibroblast line MRC-5, and the embryonic carcinoma cell line 2102Ep, which is known to express high levels of endogenous L1HS-Ta (Leibold et al., 1990).
evidence: This describes the cell lines used in the study and is supported by citations.

claim: The 2102Ep cell line is known to express high levels of endogenous L1HS-Ta.
source: and the embryonic carcinoma cell line 2102Ep, which is known to express high levels of endogenous L1HS-Ta (Leibold et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leibold et al., 1990.

claim: ORF1p expression is consistent with the proportion of human tumors expressing ORF1p.
source: We detected ORF1p expression in whole cell extracts of half of the transformed cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with the proportion of human tumors expressing ORF1p (Rodić et al., 2014) and with previous work (Belancio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data and citations to Rodić et al., 2014 and Belancio et al., 2010.

claim: ORF1p was faintly detected in two additional transformed cell lines (HeLa S3, Hep G2) after L1 RNP enrichment.
source: We observed similar results as in whole cell extracts, except that ORF1p was faintly detected in two additional transformed cell lines (HeLa S3, Hep G2, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The study used RNA-seq reads mapped on the L1HS consensus sequence to estimate the proportion of L1 transcripts originating from the L1HS-Ta subfamily.
source: In a complementary approach, we estimated the proportion of L1 transcripts originating from the L1HS-Ta subfamily by counting RNA-seq reads mapped on the L1HS consensus sequence, which encompass subfamily-diagnostic SNPs in the L1 3' UTR sequence (ACA for L1HS-Ta, ACG for L1HS-PreTa and GAG for L1PA2 and older) (Boissinot et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the methodology used and is supported by citation to Boissinot et al., 2000.

claim: In several transformed cells and in hESC, L1HS-Ta retrotransposons can escape the epigenetic, transcriptional and post-transcriptional controls that usually limit their expression in most somatic cells.
source: Altogether these data indicate that, in several - but not all - transformed cells and in hESC, L1HS-Ta retrotransposons can escape the epigenetic, transcriptional and post-transcriptional controls that usually limit their expression in most somatic cells (Faulkner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the ORF1p and RNA-seq data and is consistent with Faulkner et al., 2009.

claim: The study adapted the ATLAS method for deep sequencing to map genomic locations of L1HS-Ta elements.
source: To achieve this task, we adapted for deep sequencing an existing method termed ATLAS (Badge et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the methodology used and is supported by citation to Badge et al., 2003.

claim: ATLAS-seq relies on random mechanical fragmentation of genomic DNA to ensure high-coverage.
source: In brief, ATLAS-seq relies on the random mechanical fragmentation of the genomic DNA to ensure high-coverage, ligation of adapter sequences, suppression PCR-amplification of L1HS-Ta element junctions, and Ion Torrent sequencing using single-end 400 bp read chemistry (Figure 2a–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, see also Materials and methods section).
evidence: This describes the ATLAS-seq methodology.

claim: ATLAS-seq combines amplification and mapping of L1 downstream flanking sequence as well as the L1 upstream flanking sequence of full length elements.
source: A notable aspect of ATLAS-seq is that we combine amplification and mapping of L1 downstream flanking sequence as well as the L1 upstream flanking sequence of full length elements (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This describes the ATLAS-seq methodology shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: ATLAS-seq allows the unambiguous identification of full-length and potentially retrotransposition-competent genomic instances.
source: This allows the unambiguous identification of full-length and potentially retrotransposition-competent genomic instances.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATLAS-seq methodology that maps both 5' and 3' ends of L1 elements.

claim: The 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions correspond to 1633 distinct loci.
source: In total, ATLAS-seq identified 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions in the 12 cell lines analyzed, corresponding to 1633 distinct loci and including 358 full length elements (22%) (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the ATLAS-seq experimental data.

claim: The 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions include 358 full length elements (22%).
source: In total, ATLAS-seq identified 7823 high-confidence L1HS-Ta insertions in the 12 cell lines analyzed, corresponding to 1633 distinct loci and including 358 full length elements (22%) (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the ATLAS-seq experimental data.

claim: Each cell line contains on average 178 (±12) full-length L1HS-Ta elements.
source: On average (± s.d.), each cell line contains 652 (±68) L1HS-Ta copies, including 178 (±12) full-length elements.
evidence: This is directly supported by the ATLAS-seq experimental data.

claim: 72 non-reference insertions identified in HEK-293T cells were randomly selected for PCR validation.
source: To further validate the L1HS-Ta elements mapped by ATLAS-seq, we randomly selected and tested by PCR 72 non-reference insertions identified in HEK-293T cells with a broad range of supporting ATLAS-seq reads.
evidence: This describes the validation experiments performed.

claim: Primers could be designed for 70/72 loci selected for validation.
source: Primers could be designed for 70/72 loci.
evidence: This describes the validation experiments performed.

claim: 66/70 of the tested L1HS-Ta were validated by PCR.
source: We validated 66/70 of the tested L1HS-Ta, giving a true positive rate of 94% (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by PCR validation experiments.

claim: L1HS-Ta elements are highly polymorphic and contribute to the diversity of the human genome.
source: Collectively, these data reinforce the notion that L1HS-Ta elements are highly polymorphic and contribute to the diversity of the human genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATLAS-seq data showing extensive polymorphism among cell lines.

claim: The transcriptional activity of the L1 promoter might be influenced by its immediate upstream genomic sequence.
source: This model is consistent with previous observations made on few L1 instances suggesting that the transcriptional activity of the L1 promoter might be influenced by its immediate upstream genomic sequence (Lavie et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lavie et al., 2004.

claim: The presence or absence of polymorphic L1s at permissive loci may represent risk factors for particular cancer types.
source: We note that the presence or absence of polymorphic L1s at these permissive loci, and their degree of transcriptional activation, may represent risk factors for particular cancer types, and more specific biomarkers than global L1 expression or methylation status.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study.

claim: The study provides near-complete maps of L1HS-Ta elements present in widely used normal and transformed model cell lines.
source: Furthermore, we provide here a unique resource consisting of near-complete maps of L1HS-Ta elements present in widely used normal and transformed model cell lines, for which the availability of genomic datasets is regularly increasing (including several tier-1 & tier-2 cell-lines of the ENCODE project).
evidence: This describes the resource provided by the study.

claim: These L1 maps will be of broad utility to address the impact and regulation of transposable elements in the human genome.
source: These maps will be of broad utility in the future to address the impact and regulation of transposable elements in the human genome.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the future utility of the resource.

claim: Isolated RNA-seq and ChIP-seq signals resulting from the presence of non-reference L1 copies can only be correctly interpreted if L1 maps are available.
source: Indeed, isolated RNA-seq and ChIP-seq signals resulting from the presence of non-reference L1 copies can only be correctly interpreted if such maps are available.
evidence: This is logical inference about the utility of the L1 maps.

claim: The L1 maps can act as a platform to fully interpret and profit from the many expanding public datasets generated using the same cell lines.
source: Thus they can act as a platform to fully interpret and profit from the many expanding public datasets generated using the same cell lines.
evidence: This is logical inference about the utility of the L1 maps.

claim: The study extends the concept of retrotransposition-competent L1 copies to the transcriptional regulation of each individual locus and cell type.
source: Therefore, we extend the concept of retrotransposition-competent L1 copies, previously described as 'hot L1s' (Brouha et al., 2003; Beck et al., 2010), to the transcriptional regulation of each individual locus and cell type.
evidence: This is a conceptual extension based on the findings of the study and is supported by citations.

claim: Activation of L1 transcription in somatic cells is governed by individual-, locus-, and cell-type-specific determinants.
source: Overall, our data suggest that activation of L1 transcription in somatic cells is governed by individual-, locus-, and cell-type-specific determinants and provide a framework to study how distinct L1HS-Ta copies may be regulated by environmental, physiological and pathological triggers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive data showing differential L1 expression patterns.

claim: Future work will determine the factors and cellular signaling pathways that contribute to the transcriptional reactivation of different L1HS-Ta copies in somatic cells.
source: Future work will determine the factors and cellular signaling pathways that contribute to the transcriptional reactivation of the different L1HS-Ta copies in somatic cells.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: The HEK-293 cell line is a clonal derivative of primary human embryonic kidney cells transformed with Adenovirus 5 (Ad5) DNA.
source: The HEK-293 cell line is a clonal derivative of primary human embryonic kidney cells transformed with Adenovirus 5 (Ad5) DNA (Graham et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Graham et al., 1977.

claim: The HEK-293T cell line is a clonal derivative of HEK-293 cells stably transfected with a temperature sensitive SV40 Large T antigen allele and the neomycin resistance gene.
source: The HEK-293T cell line (also known as 293T or 293/tsA1609neo) is a clonal derivative of HEK-293 cells stably transfected with a temperature sensitive SV40 Large T antigen allele and the neomycin resistance gene (DuBridge et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DuBridge et al., 1987.

claim: All cell cultures tested negative for mycoplasma infection.
source: All above-mentioned cell cultures tested negative for mycoplasma infection using the MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Lonza, Basel, Switzerland).
evidence: This describes quality control measures for the cell cultures.

claim: Cell line authenticity was verified by multiplex STR analysis.
source: Cell line authenticity was verified by multiplex STR analysis (PowerPlex 21 PCR system [Promega, Madison, WI], assays performed by Eurofins Genomics [Ebersberg, Germany] as a service provider) and comparison with the DSMZ database (https://www.dsmz.de/services/services-human-and-animal-cell-lines/online-str-analysis.html) or with previously published profiles for H1 and 2102Ep cells (Josephson et al., 2007; Mallon et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes quality control measures for the cell lines and is supported by citations.

claim: Only 1 element out of 10 belonging to characterized L1 lineages was ranked among the top 20 most highly expressed L1 copies.
source: In total, only 1 element out of 10, inserted in the NEDD4 gene (EXP_ID_0447), was ranked among the top 20 most highly expressed L1 copies.
evidence: This is supported by the lineage analysis and expression data.

claim: The high level of expression of a small cohort of L1 insertions is not an intrinsic feature of any previously identified lineage.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that the observed high level of expression of a small cohort of L1 insertions is not an intrinsic feature of any previously identified lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage analysis showing that most highly expressed L1s do not belong to known hot lineages.

claim: The L1 copy EXP_ID_0447 in the NEDD4 gene is retrotransposition-competent.
source: For this particular copy, we confirmed the presence of the typical RP transduction by Sanger sequencing. Consistent with its affiliation to the 'hot' L1 RP lineage, this copy is also retrotransposition-competent (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by the retrotransposition assay shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The proportion of expressed L1 insertions in genes was slightly higher than that of non-expressed copies, but the difference was not significant.
source: Although the proportion of expressed L1s in genes was slightly higher than that of non-expressed copies, the difference was not significant.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of genomic location data.

claim: The proportion of L1 copies in antisense orientation was not significantly different between expressed and non-expressed copies.
source: However, this proportion was not significantly different between expressed and non-expressed copies.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of L1 orientation data.

claim: Expressed L1 copies were not significantly enriched in amplified regions.
source: The majority of L1 copies were inserted in normal regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b), whether they were expressed or not, and expressed L1 copies were not significantly enriched in amplified regions.
evidence: This is supported by the copy number variation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b.

claim: 5 out of the 20 most highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies fulfill at least two criteria strongly supporting their ability to retrotranspose.
source: We found that 5 out of the 20 most highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies across all cell lines fulfill at least two of these criteria strongly supporting their ability to retrotranspose and 6 additional ones could be identified as progenitors of other, daughter copies.
evidence: This is supported by the combined analysis of cellular assays, 3' transduction data, and published data.

claim: 6 additional highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies could be identified as progenitors of other, daughter copies.
source: We found that 5 out of the 20 most highly-expressed L1HS-Ta copies across all cell lines fulfill at least two of these criteria strongly supporting their ability to retrotranspose and 6 additional ones could be identified as progenitors of other, daughter copies.
evidence: This is supported by the 3' transduction analysis.

claim: The remaining nine highly-expressed elements could also be retrotransposition-competent, but have not been tested in cultured assays, nor could daughter L1 copies be unambiguously identified.
source: The remaining nine elements could also be retrotransposition-competent, but have not been tested in cultured assays, nor could daughter L1 copies be unambiguously identified.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the retrotransposition competence analysis.

claim: The embryonal carcinoma cells 2102Ep accumulate comparable global levels of L1HS-Ta transcripts to MCF7 cells.
source: As compared to MCF7 cells, the embryonal carcinoma cells 2102Ep accumulate comparable global levels of L1HS-Ta transcripts, but seem to have a higher number of permissive L1HS-Ta loci, each contributing to a smaller proportion of the total
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data comparing MCF7 and 2102Ep cells.

claim: 2102Ep cells seem to have a higher number of permissive L1HS-Ta loci than MCF7 cells, each contributing to a smaller proportion of the total.
source: As compared to MCF7 cells, the embryonal carcinoma cells 2102Ep accumulate comparable global levels of L1HS-Ta transcripts, but seem to have a higher number of permissive L1HS-Ta loci, each contributing to a smaller proportion of the total, although the number of active instances still represents a small fraction (<10%) of all L1HS-Ta copies in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data comparing MCF7 and 2102Ep cells.

claim: The number of active L1HS-Ta instances in 2102Ep cells still represents a small fraction (<10%) of all L1HS-Ta copies.
source: although the number of active instances still represents a small fraction (<10%) of all L1HS-Ta copies in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data for 2102Ep cells.
